Define $L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ by\\n    44\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    45\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:cl-dlnf}\\n    46\\t\\t\\tL_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}(u,s,v) = \\\\bigl(L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),\\\\, s,\\\\, \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)\\\\bigr)\\\\;,\\n    47\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    48\\t\\twhere $i = \\\\chi(s)$ and $\\\\pi_{i-1}$ zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input. The function $L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the concatenation of (i) the identity on $V_I$, (ii) for each $i$ the $1$-level CL function $v \\\\mapsto \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ on $V_V$, and (iii) for each pair $(s,v') \\\\in V_I \\\\oplus V_V$ the $1$-level CL function $L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{v'}$ on $V_X$; thus $L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is a $3$-level CL function.\\n    49\\t\\n    50\\t\\tThe question distribution of $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$ is the typed CL distribution obtained as follows: sample a type pair $(t_{\\\\mathrm A}, t_{\\\\mathrm B})$ uniformly from $\\\\mathcal T^{\\\\mathrm{ld}} \\\\times \\\\mathcal T^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$, sample $z = (u,s,v)$ uniformly from $V$, and send each player $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$ the question $(t_w, L_{t_w}(z))$.\\n    51\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n    52\\t\\n    53\\tThe next two lemmas show that the CL functions $L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}$, $L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$, $L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ give rise to the axis-parallel and diagonal line-versus-point distributions.\\n    54\\t\\n    55\\t\\\\begin{lemma}\\\\label{lem:alnf}\\n    56\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\\n    57\\t\\tConsider the pair $(\\\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\\\bigl((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0)\\\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\\\ell = \\\\ell(u_0, e_i)$ where $i = \\\\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\\\F_q^m$, and $\\\\ell$ is a line that goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,m\\\\}$.\\n    58\\t\\\\end{lemma}\\n    59\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n    60\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:line-representative}\\n    61\\t\\tSince $s$ is uniformly random in $\\\\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$, the index $i = \\\\chi(s)$ is uniformly random in $\\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,m\\\\}$, so $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\\\\ell(u_0,e_i)$. Since $u_0 = L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{e_i}(u)$ is the canonical representative of the line through $u$ in direction $e_i$, we have $u \\\\in \\\\ell(u_0,e_i)$.\\n    62\\t\\\\end{proof}\\n    63\\t\\n    64\\t\\\\begin{lemma}\\\\label{lem:dlnf}\\n    65\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:line}\\n    66\\t\\tConsider the pair $(\\\\ell, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the tuple $\\\\bigl((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0)\\\\bigr)$ from the CL distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$, and let $\\\\ell = \\\\ell(u_0, v)$ where $i = \\\\chi(s)$. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\\\F_q^m$, and $\\\\ell$ is a random diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares its first $i-1$ coordinates with $u$, for uniformly random $i \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,m\\\\}$.\\n    67\\t\\\\end{lemma}\\n    68\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n    69\\t\\t\\\\uses{lem:alnf}\\n    70\\t\\tThe proof is identical to that of Lemma~\\\\ref{lem:alnf}: uniformity of $s$ makes $i = \\\\chi(s)$ uniform, the direction component of the sampled tuple is $\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ for uniform $v$ (so its first $i-1$ coordinates vanish), and $u_0 = L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u)$ places $u$ on the line $\\\\ell(u_0,\\\\pi_{i-1}(v))$.\\n    71\\t\\\\end{proof}\\n    72\\t\\n    73\\t\\\\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]\\\\label{def:line-point-dist}\\n    74\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, lem:alnf, lem:dlnf}\\n    75\\t\\tThe \\\\emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\\\ell = (u_0,e_i),\\\\, u)$, where we omit the $0$ components for simplicity. The \\\\emph{diagonal line-point distribution} $D_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$ is the distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\\\ell = (u_0,s,v),\\\\, u)$. The \\\\emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\\\\mathsf{Line}}$ is the equal mixture of the two: with probability $\\\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$, and with probability $\\\\tfrac12$ output a sample from $D_{\\\\mathsf{DLine}}$.\\n    76\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n    77\\t\\n    78\\t\\\\begin{definition}[Win predicate of the classical low individual degree game]\\\\label{def:ld-win-predicate}\\n    79\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:line, def:polyfunc}\\n    80\\t\\tFix $\\\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$. Answers in the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.\\n    81\\t\\t\\\\begin{itemize}\\n    82\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{Point}$, question content $u \\\\in \\\\F_q^m$: the answer is an element of $\\\\F_q^k$.\\n    83\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{ALine}$, question content $(u_0,s) \\\\in \\\\F_q^m \\\\times \\\\F_q$, specifying the axis-parallel line $\\\\ell(u_0,e_i)$ with $i = \\\\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple $(f_1,\\\\ldots,f_k)$ of univariate polynomials $f_j\\\\colon \\\\F_q \\\\to \\\\F_q$ of degree at most $d$, each given by its $d+1$ coefficients.\\n    84\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{DLine}$, question content $(u_0,s,v) \\\\in \\\\F_q^m \\\\times \\\\F_q \\\\times \\\\F_q^m$, specifying the diagonal line $\\\\ell(u_0,v')$ with $v' = \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\\\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple of univariate polynomials of degree at most $md$.\\n    85\\t\\t\\\\end{itemize}\\n    86\\t\\tThe win predicate $D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}} = D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\\\\mathrm A}, x_{\\\\mathrm A}, t_{\\\\mathrm B}, x_{\\\\mathrm B}, a_{\\\\mathrm A}, a_{\\\\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts.\\n    87\\t\\t\\\\begin{enumerate}\\n    88\\t\\t\\t\\\\item (\\\\textbf{Consistency test}) If $t_{\\\\mathrm A} = t_{\\\\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\\\\mathrm A} = a_{\\\\mathrm B}$.\\n    89\\t\\t\\t% The source phrases both clauses with \\\"the\\\" t such that x = u_0 + tv; that phrase\\n    90\\t\\t\\t% does not determine t on diagonal questions with direction v' = 0, which the\\n    91\\t\\t\\t% question distribution samples with positive probability. The universal\\n    92\\t\\t\\t% quantification over t used here is the local correction; see the remark below.\\n    93\\t\\t\\t\\\\item (\\\\textbf{Axis-parallel line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\\\mathsf{ALine}$ and $t_{\\\\overline w} = \\\\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,k\\\\}$ and all $t \\\\in \\\\F_q$ such that $x_{\\\\overline w} = u_0 + t e_i$, where $i = \\\\chi(s)$.\\n    94\\t\\t\\t\\\\item (\\\\textbf{Diagonal line-versus-point test}) If $t_w = \\\\mathsf{DLine}$ and $t_{\\\\overline w} = \\\\mathsf{Point}$, accept if and only if $f_j(t) = (a_{\\\\overline w})_j$ for all $j \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,k\\\\}$ and all $t \\\\in \\\\F_q$ such that $x_{\\\\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$, where $v' = \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\\\chi(s)$.\\n    95\\t\\t\\\\end{enumerate}\\n    96\\t\\tThe game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the typed game with type set $\\\\mathcal T^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$, the question distribution of Definition~\\\\ref{def:ld-question-distribution}, and win predicate $D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$.\\n    97\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n    98\\t\\n    99\\t\\\\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\\\\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}\\n   100\\t\\tThe source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \\\\in \\\\F_q$ such that $x_{\\\\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\\\\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\\\\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \\\\mapsto u_0 + t \\\\cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$.\\n   101\\t\\\\end{remark}\\n   102\\t\\n   103\\tThe soundness properties of the low individual degree game are expressed in terms of the following class of measurements.\\n   104\\t\\n   105\\t\\\\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]\\\\label{def:ld-meas}\\n   106\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:polyfunc, def:polymeasurements, def:polynomials-degree}\\n   107\\t\\tLet $\\\\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ denote the set of POVM measurements indexed by $\\\\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, the polynomial representatives of individual degree at most $d$ in each variable; this is the notion of Definition~\\\\ref{def:polymeasurements}, and the argument order $(m,q,d)$ follows that definition (the paper orders the arguments as $(m,d,q)$). By Definition~\\\\ref{def:polynomials-degree}, evaluation identifies these representatives with the corresponding polynomial functions $g\\\\colon \\\\F_q^m \\\\to \\\\F_q$, bijectively whenever $d \\\\le q-1$; the parameter regimes of this chapter (Definition~\\\\ref{def:introparams} fixes $d = 1$, and admissibility gives $q \\\\ge 2$) always satisfy this. More generally, for an integer $k$ and tuples $m = (m_1,\\\\ldots,m_k)$, $q = (q_1,\\\\ldots,q_k)$, $d = (d_1,\\\\ldots,d_k)$, let $\\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$ denote the set of measurements $G = \\\\{G_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k}\\\\}$ such that for each $i \\\\in \\\\{1,\\\\ldots,k\\\\}$, the outcome index $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i\\\\colon \\\\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \\\\to \\\\F_{q_i}$ of individual degree at most $d_i$.\\n   108\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n   109\\t\\n   110\\tQuantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \\\\emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. Instead, the construction relies on the low \\\\emph{individual} degree test, whose quantum soundness is proved in~\\\\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} and generalized in~\\\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.\\n   111\\t\\n   112\\t% The paper states this result in a theorem environment with the label lem:ld-soundness.\\n   113\\t% We keep both the environment and the label verbatim for cross-reference fidelity.\\n   114\\t\\\\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree test]\\\\label{lem:ld-soundness}\\n   115\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:projective-strategy-general, def:tensor-product-value, def:povm-distance, def:bracket}\\n   116\\t\\tThere exists a function\\n   117\\t\\t\\\\[\\n   118\\t\\t\\t\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}(\\\\eps, q, m, d, k) = a\\\\,(dmk)^a \\\\bigl(\\\\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\\\\bigr)\\n   119\\t\\t\\\\]\\n   120\\t\\tfor universal constants $a \\\\ge 1$ and $0 < b \\\\le 1$ such that the following holds. For all $\\\\eps > 0$ and every parameter tuple $\\\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ as in Definition~\\\\ref{def:ld-game} (so $q$ is an admissible field size and $m$ divides $q$), and for all projective strategies $(\\\\psi, A, B)$ that succeed with probability at least $1-\\\\eps$ in the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$, there exist measurements\\n   121\\t\\t\\\\[\\n   122\\t\\t\\tG^w \\\\in \\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)\\n   123\\t\\t\\\\]\\n   124\\t\\ton $\\\\hilb_w$ for $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$, where by slight abuse of notation $m$, $q$, $d$ denote the constant tuples $(m,\\\\ldots,m)$, $(q,\\\\ldots,q)$, $(d,\\\\ldots,d)$ of length $k$, such that\\n   125\\t\\t\\\\begin{align*}\\n   126\\t\\t\\tA^{\\\\mathsf{Point},\\\\, u}_{a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   127\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   128\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot G^{\\\\mathrm B}_{[(g_1(u),\\\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k)]}\\\\;,\\\\\\\\\\n   129\\t\\t\\tG^{\\\\mathrm A}_{[(g_1(u),\\\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k)]} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   130\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   131\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot B^{\\\\mathsf{Point},\\\\, u}_{a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k}\\\\;,\\\\\\\\\\n   132\\t\\t\\tG^{\\\\mathrm A}_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   133\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   134\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot G^{\\\\mathrm B}_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k}\\\\;,\\n   135\\t\\t\\\\end{align*}\\n   136\\t\\twhere $\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}} = \\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}(\\\\eps,q,m,d,k)$, all three approximations are with respect to the state $\\\\ket{\\\\psi}$, and the bracket notation for post-processed outcomes is that of Definition~\\\\ref{def:bracket}. The first two approximations hold on average over the uniform distribution on $u \\\\in \\\\F_q^m$; no question distribution is associated with the third.\\n   137\\t\\\\end{theorem}\\n   138\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n   139\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:povm-distance}\\n   140\\t\\tLet $\\\\Sigma = \\\\F_q$ and let $\\\\code \\\\subseteq \\\\Sigma^q$ be the Reed--Solomon code of degree $d$: the set of all $(p(x_1),\\\\ldots,p(x_q))$ where $p\\\\colon \\\\F_q \\\\to \\\\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\\\\ldots,x_q$ enumerate $\\\\F_q$. We may assume $d < q$. In the opposite regime the statement is immediate: for $k \\\\ge 1$ and $d \\\\ge q$ the prefactor gives $\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}} \\\\ge a\\\\,(dmk)^a\\\\, q^{-b} \\\\ge q^{a-b} \\\\ge 1$, while the quantity bounded in Definition~\\\\ref{def:povm-distance} never exceeds $2$ for families of POVM elements, so the three approximations hold for an arbitrary choice of $G^w \\\\in \\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$; and for $k = 0$ every answer tuple is empty, all measurements involved are single-outcome, and the approximations hold with error zero. With the\\n   142\\t\\t% intended value n = q the printed distance q-d+1 exceeds the true minimum distance\\n   143\\t\\t% q-d of the degree-d evaluation code, and the dimension claim d+1 requires d < q.\\n   144\\t\\t% Both points are corrected above; the regime d >= q, which the parameter tuple of\\n   145\\t\\t% Definition def:ld-game permits, is handled by the triviality argument.\\n   146\\t\\tThe two-prover tensor-code test for the code $\\\\code^{\\\\ot m}$, as described in Figures~1 and~2 of~\\\\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, coincides with the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}$ with parameters $\\\\mathsf{ldparams}$ and $k=1$: the axis-parallel line-versus-point test is their axis-parallel lines test, with the roles of the two players chosen uniformly at random, which is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor-code test from Section~4.1 there; the diagonal line-versus-point test is their subcube commutation test, again with the added symmetrization between the players; and the consistency test is their synchronicity test. Define $L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}$ to be the $1$-level CL function on $V$ that projects onto $V_X$: for every $(u,s,v) \\\\in V$,\\n    29\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    30\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:cl-ptf}\\n    31\\t\\t\\tL_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}(u,s,v) = (u,0,0)\\\\;.\\n    32\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    33\\t\\tFor $s \\\\in \\\\F_q$, let $\\\\chi(s)$ be the unique integer such that\\n    34\\t\\t\\\\begin{equation}\\n    35\\t\\t\\t\\\\label{eq:chi-func}\\n    36\\t\\t\\ts = (\\\\chi(s)-1)\\\\,\\\\frac{q}{m} + r\\n    37\\t\\t\\\\end{equation}\\n    38\\t\\tfor some $0 \\\\le r < q/m$, where $s$ is interpreted as an integer in $\\\\{0,1,\\\\ldots,q-1\\\\}$ under the identification of $\\\\F_q$ with binary strings fixed in Chapter~\\\\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra}. Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\\\\F_q^m$, and $\\\\ell$ is a random diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares its first $i-1$ coordinates with $u$, for uniformly random $i \\\\in \\\\{1,2,\\\\ldots,m\\\\}$.\\n    67\\t\\\\end{lemma}\\n    68\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n    69\\t\\t\\\\uses{lem:alnf}\\n    70\\t\\tThe proof is identical to that of Lemma~\\\\ref{lem:alnf}: uniformity of $s$ makes $i = \\\\chi(s)$ uniform, the direction component of the sampled tuple is $\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ for uniform $v$ (so its first $i-1$ coordinates vanish), and $u_0 = L^{\\\\mathrm{Ln}}_{\\\\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u)$ places $u$ on the line $\\\\ell(u_0,\\\\pi_{i-1}(v))$.\\n    71\\t\\\\end{proof}\\n    72\\t\\n    73\\t\\\\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]\\\\label{def:line-point-dist}\\n    74\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, lem:alnf, lem:dlnf}\\n    75\\t\\tThe \\\\emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}$ is the distribution $\\\\mu_{L_{\\\\mathsf{ALine}}, L_{\\\\mathsf{Point}}}$ over pairs $(\\\\ell = (u_0,e_i),\\\\, u)$, where we omit the $0$ components for simplicity. Answers in the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.\\n    81\\t\\t\\\\begin{itemize}\\n    82\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{Point}$, question content $u \\\\in \\\\F_q^m$: the answer is an element of $\\\\F_q^k$.\\n    83\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{ALine}$, question content $(u_0,s) \\\\in \\\\F_q^m \\\\times \\\\F_q$, specifying the axis-parallel line $\\\\ell(u_0,e_i)$ with $i = \\\\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple $(f_1,\\\\ldots,f_k)$ of univariate polynomials $f_j\\\\colon \\\\F_q \\\\to \\\\F_q$ of degree at most $d$, each given by its $d+1$ coefficients.\\n    84\\t\\t\\t\\\\item Type $\\\\mathsf{DLine}$, question content $(u_0,s,v) \\\\in \\\\F_q^m \\\\times \\\\F_q \\\\times \\\\F_q^m$, specifying the diagonal line $\\\\ell(u_0,v')$ with $v' = \\\\pi_{i-1}(v)$ and $i = \\\\chi(s)$: the answer is a $k$-tuple of univariate polynomials of degree at most $md$.\\n    85\\t\\t\\\\end{itemize}\\n    86\\t\\tThe win predicate $D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}} = D^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$ is the function of the tuple $(t_{\\\\mathrm A}, x_{\\\\mathrm A}, t_{\\\\mathrm B}, x_{\\\\mathrm B}, a_{\\\\mathrm A}, a_{\\\\mathrm B})$ determined by the following clauses, evaluated for $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$; in all cases where no action is indicated, the predicate accepts.\\n    87\\t\\t\\\\begin{enumerate}\\n    88\\t\\t\\t\\\\item (\\\\textbf{Consistency test}) If $t_{\\\\mathrm A} = t_{\\\\mathrm B}$, accept if and only if $a_{\\\\mathrm A} = a_{\\\\mathrm B}$.\\n    89\\t\\t\\t% The source phrases both clauses with \\\"the\\\" t such that x = u_0 + tv; that phrase\\n    90\\t\\t\\t% does not determine t on diagonal questions with direction v' = 0, which the\\n    91\\t\\t\\t% question distribution samples with positive probability. More generally, for an integer $k$ and tuples $m = (m_1,\\\\ldots,m_k)$, $q = (q_1,\\\\ldots,q_k)$, $d = (d_1,\\\\ldots,d_k)$, let $\\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$ denote the set of measurements $G = \\\\{G_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k}\\\\}$ such that for each $i \\\\in \\\\{1,\\\\ldots,k\\\\}$, the outcome index $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i\\\\colon \\\\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \\\\to \\\\F_{q_i}$ of individual degree at most $d_i$.\\n   108\\t\\\\end{definition}\\n   109\\t\\n   110\\tQuantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \\\\emph{total} degree was claimed by Natarajan and Vidick, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test by Vidick; there is a known gap in the soundness analysis of that test, and it is not used here. The statement below is the form most directly useful in what follows.\\n   111\\t\\n   112\\t% The paper states this result in a theorem environment with the label lem:ld-soundness.\\n   113\\t% We keep both the environment and the label verbatim for cross-reference fidelity.\\n   114\\t\\\\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low individual degree test]\\\\label{lem:ld-soundness}\\n   115\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-game, def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:projective-strategy-general, def:tensor-product-value, def:povm-distance, def:bracket}\\n   116\\t\\tThere exists a function\\n   117\\t\\t\\\\[\\n   118\\t\\t\\t\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}(\\\\eps, q, m, d, k) = a\\\\,(dmk)^a \\\\bigl(\\\\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\\\\bigr)\\n   119\\t\\t\\\\]\\n   120\\t\\tfor universal constants $a \\\\ge 1$ and $0 < b \\\\le 1$ such that the following holds. For all $\\\\eps > 0$ and every parameter tuple $\\\\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$ as in Definition~\\\\ref{def:ld-game} (so $q$ is an admissible field size and $m$ divides $q$), and for all projective strategies $(\\\\psi, A, B)$ that succeed with probability at least $1-\\\\eps$ in the game $\\\\mathcal G^{\\\\mathrm{ld}}_{\\\\mathsf{ldparams}}$, there exist measurements\\n   121\\t\\t\\\\[\\n   122\\t\\t\\tG^w \\\\in \\\\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)\\n   123\\t\\t\\\\]\\n   124\\t\\ton $\\\\hilb_w$ for $w \\\\in \\\\{\\\\mathrm A,\\\\mathrm B\\\\}$, where by slight abuse of notation $m$, $q$, $d$ denote the constant tuples $(m,\\\\ldots,m)$, $(q,\\\\ldots,q)$, $(d,\\\\ldots,d)$ of length $k$, such that\\n   125\\t\\t\\\\begin{align*}\\n   126\\t\\t\\tA^{\\\\mathsf{Point},\\\\, u}_{a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   127\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   128\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot G^{\\\\mathrm B}_{[(g_1(u),\\\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k)]}\\\\;,\\\\\\\\\\n   129\\t\\t\\tG^{\\\\mathrm A}_{[(g_1(u),\\\\ldots,g_k(u)) = (a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k)]} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   130\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   131\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot B^{\\\\mathsf{Point},\\\\, u}_{a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k}\\\\;,\\\\\\\\\\n   132\\t\\t\\tG^{\\\\mathrm A}_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k} \\\\ot I_{\\\\mathrm B}\\n   133\\t\\t\\t&\\\\approx_{\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}}\\n   134\\t\\t\\tI_{\\\\mathrm A} \\\\ot G^{\\\\mathrm B}_{g_1,\\\\ldots,g_k}\\\\;,\\n   135\\t\\t\\\\end{align*}\\n   136\\t\\twhere $\\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}} = \\\\delta_{\\\\mathrm{ld}}(\\\\eps,q,m,d,k)$, all three approximations are with respect to the state $\\\\ket{\\\\psi}$, and the bracket notation for post-processed outcomes is that of Definition~\\\\ref{def:bracket}. The first two approximations hold on average over the uniform distribution on $u \\\\in \\\\F_q^m$; no question distribution is associated with the third.\\n   137\\t\\\\end{theorem}\\n   138\\t\\\\begin{proof}\\n   139\\t\\t\\\\uses{def:ld-question-distribution, def:ld-win-predicate, def:ld-meas, def:povm-distance}\\n   140\\t\\tLet $\\\\Sigma = \\\\F_q$ and let $\\\\code \\\\subseteq \\\\Sigma^q$ be the Reed--Solomon code of degree $d$: the set of all $(p(x_1),\\\\ldots,p(x_q))$ where $p\\\\colon \\\\F_q \\\\to \\\\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\\\\ldots,x_q$ enumerate $\\\\F_q$.
